newsitem.title: UK: Political spat fails to dampen market's EMU ardour.
newsitem.headline: Political spat fails to dampen market's EMU ardour.

text.p: Jacques Chirac's doubts that Italy will make it to the EMU starting blocks in January 1999 have given markets a further clue on the extent of worries about the budget position of the so-called "Club Med" countries.

The French President's remarks infuriated the Italians but, despite the underlying political tension, failed to prompt much reaction in financial markets because of reluctance to unwind profitable convergence trades.

Analysts say convergence trades -- which bet on the likelihood that the economies and financial instruments of candidates for European economic and monetary union (EMU) will converge successfully -- have dominated for much of this year.

This is due to belief the political will in "core" European countries like Germany and France is strong enough to force European monetary union (EMU) through on time -- albeit with smoke and mirrors regarding the Maastricht criteria and some creative accounting to get budget deficits down.
"People are afraid of losing money and divergence trades cost you money," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

"The market believes that at the moment it can make more money with convergence trades. It's got nothing to do with economics and it's got nothing to do with whether the politicians are right or wrong."
At present there is no talk now of delay or watering down the criteria much and analysts note a big sea-change in the way the debate has developed over the past couple of weeks.

This is why the market has been, and is currently, reluctant to bet against EMU. Germany holds the key, and if it is happy to line up with Italy, Spain and Portugal on the starting grid for EMU then current market moves are justified. If it is not, and a high ranking German official said so publically and definitely, then the EMU bubble could burst.

German officials have said they are not too happy with the way fiscal deficits are being pared and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl has said the single currency would probably begin with only five to seven European Union members.

This would not include Italy, Spain or Portugal, who are part of the "Club Med". Analysts believe the most likely members at the launch of EMU will be Germany, France, Austria, Luxembourg, Belgium and the Netherlands -- with Ireland and Finland making up the seven that Kohl has in mind.

"Why would Germany say yes to something that is so self evidentially against the interests of stable countries like Germany and France?" said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS in London.

He warned that while everyone is euphoric about EMU going ahead on time, there is going to be a wake-up call somewhere along the line. "It is going to be a long, long time before Italy, Spain and Portugal go in," he said.

Even if it turns out that core Europe does not what to see the Italian cuckoo in the EMU nest it certainly wants to see the lira perch in the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) for a while at a rate that will prevent Italy continuing to benefit from its competitive exchange rate.

Joe Prendergast, forex strategist at Merrill Lynch, said while the lira has recovered from its 1992 collapse it remains theoretically under-valued by about six percent against the French franc and about 13 percent versus the mark.

"It is possible France believes Italy should re-enter the ERM at a rate that corrects more of this competitive advantage accrued by Italy since 1992," he said. Merrill's current estimate of long-run purchasing power parity (PPP) would imply a mark/lira central rate around 940.00, over five percent above its current level.
